title: The $533 Million Factory That Made Nothing
hook: Government pays for defense capacity as it is built, not after it works. When the plant never produces, the taxpayer has already footed the bill.
key_points: ProPublica reports taxpayers funded a $533 million artillery plant, built with General Dynamics, that produced nothing.
Defense contracts often reimburse costs and progress rather than delivered output, so money moves before results do.
Sole-source and urgent-need procurement weakens the main discipline on contractors: the threat of losing the work.
Because capacity projects are strategic, cancelling one is politically costly even when it is failing.
Accountability then depends on audit and journalism after the fact, not on competition during the contract.
content_html: Public procurement fails in a specific, repeatable way, and defense manufacturing shows it most starkly: the government often pays for capacity as it is created rather than for output once it exists. ProPublica's Jesse Coburn reports that taxpayers funded a $533 million artillery plant, built with General Dynamics, that made nothing. The striking part is not that a large project ran into trouble — large industrial projects often do — but that the financial risk of the trouble sat with the public rather than the builder.
extra_html: Three features tend to combine in cases like this. First, contract structure: reimbursing costs and construction milestones means money flows against effort, so a plant can be fully paid for before anyone learns whether it can produce. Second, weak competitive discipline. When a capability is urgent and only one or two firms can supply it, the ordinary sanction for poor performance — losing the next contract — loses its force, and the government negotiates from a position of dependence. Third, sunk-cost politics: a strategic capacity project acquires defenders in the legislature and the supply chain, so cancelling a failing one is more painful than continuing it. What remains is after-the-fact accountability — inspectors general, audits, and reporting like this — which can document waste but rarely recovers the money. The reform ideas that follow from this diagnosis are unglamorous and consistent across governments: tie payment to demonstrated output, keep at least a second qualified supplier alive, and require public reporting of milestones so failure is visible while it is still cheap to stop.

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Taxation & Public Budgets
related.hook: A government's budget is its values written in numbers — and taxation is how it raises the money to act at all. Follow the money to understand the priorities.

related.title: The Internet Subsidy Program Paying to Wire Empty Buildings

flashcards.prompt: Why can a defense contractor be paid in full for a plant that produces nothing?
flashcards.back_html: Many contracts reimburse costs and construction progress rather than delivered output, so payment tracks effort — not results.

flashcards.prompt: What did ProPublica report about the artillery plant?

choices.text: Taxpayers funded a $533 million plant that made nothing
The plant produced ammunition at twice the expected cost
The contract was cancelled before construction began

flashcards.explanation_html: ProPublica's Jesse Coburn reported the $533 million publicly funded plant produced no output at all.

flashcards.prompt: Why does urgent, sole-source procurement weaken accountability?

choices.text: Without a competitor waiting, the threat of losing the work — the main discipline on a contractor — disappears
It exempts contractors from all federal law
It shifts all financial risk onto the contractor

flashcards.explanation_html: Competition is what usually punishes poor performance. When there is only one supplier and an urgent need, the government has little leverage left.
